prompt: A magnifier user testing a keyboard-driven multi-step form should use the magnifier's mouse-tracking mode, since that's the default in most tools. True or false: this is the right mode to test with for this scenario.

config.statement: Mouse-tracking mode is the right magnifier setting to test a keyboard-driven, no-mouse form flow with.
config.rubric: Names focus-tracking as the mode that actually matches keyboard-only navigation, and explains why mouse-tracking wouldn't reflect a real magnifier user's keyboard experience.

hints: If the scenario is keyboard-driven with no mouse involved, a mode that tracks the mouse cursor wouldn't move at all as focus changes.
Match the tracking mode to how the user is actually navigating, not to the tool's default setting.
explanation: False. Mouse-tracking mode follows the pointer, which never moves during a keyboard-only flow — the magnified viewport would just sit still while focus silently moves elsewhere on the page, giving a completely misleading test. Focus-tracking mode is the one that actually mirrors a real magnifier user navigating by keyboard, panning the viewport to follow focus exactly the way Tab moves it — testing with the wrong tracking mode for the scenario can hide real defects or manufacture false ones.

prompt: A "Copy link" button shows a brief confirmation tooltip directly above the button itself, that fades after two seconds. A separate "Item saved" toast appears in the bottom-right corner of the screen, unrelated to where the user just clicked. Compare these two for a magnifier user at 300% zoom, focus-tracking mode on.
hints: One of these appears exactly where the magnified viewport already is (wherever the user just interacted); the other appears somewhere else entirely.
Focus-tracking mode follows keyboard focus specifically — does clicking "Copy link" and staying focused on it mean the viewport is already where the confirmation appears?
explanation: A strong answer distinguishes the two clearly: the "Copy link" tooltip appears directly above the button the user's focus (and the magnified viewport) is already on, so it's very likely to be seen without any special handling. The bottom-right toast appears somewhere the viewport has no reason to be, exactly the off-screen-change pattern from the lesson — a magnifier user is likely to miss it entirely unless focus is deliberately moved there or the notification is placed adjacent to the action that triggered it instead of in a fixed corner.

prompt: A user turns on Windows forced-colours mode. What's the most accurate description of what happens to the page?

options.text: Most author-specified colors (background, text, borders) get replaced with a small system palette the user chose, while layout and spacing stay the same
The entire page is converted to greyscale automatically
The browser refuses to load pages with custom CSS colors at all

hints: This is a real, deliberate accessibility setting a user turns on for contrast or light-sensitivity reasons — not a browser restriction.
Layout, spacing and non-color styling are left alone; it's specifically color properties that get overridden.
explanation: The OS substitutes a small, user-chosen system palette for most author-specified color properties, while leaving layout and spacing untouched — not greyscale, not a load failure, a deliberate and controlled color override in service of a real accessibility need someone activated on purpose.

prompt: A toggle switch shows its "on" state with a background-color change AND a visible sliding position change (the circle moves from left to right within the track). True or false: this toggle is likely to survive forced-colours mode better than one relying on background-color alone.

config.statement: A toggle that shows state through both a color change and a positional/shape change is more resilient under forced-colours mode than one using color alone.
config.rubric: Explains that the positional change is a non-color signal that survives the OS override, unlike a color-only distinguisher.

hints: Forced colours strips color properties specifically — position and shape aren't color properties.
Compare this to the checkbox example from the lesson, which had nothing but color as its distinguisher.
explanation: True. The sliding circle's position (left versus right within the track) is a layout/shape signal, not a color one, so it survives forced-colours mode even after the OS overrides the background fill. This is exactly the kind of redundant, non-color signal the lesson's checkbox example was missing — a toggle that shows state two different ways is far more resilient than one that shows it only through a fill someone else's OS setting can strip away entirely.

prompt: At what effective viewport width is the standard 400% reflow test roughly equivalent to, starting from a typical 1280px-wide desktop viewport?

options.text: Roughly 320px — about the width of a typical mobile phone screen
Roughly 1280px — zoom doesn't change the effective layout width
Roughly 640px — exactly half the starting width

hints: 1280 divided by 4 (the 400% zoom factor) gets you close to the standard test width.
This is deliberately close to a real mobile phone's screen width — that's not a coincidence.
explanation: Roughly 320px — 1280px divided by the 400% zoom factor. This is deliberately close to a real mobile phone's viewport width, which is exactly why a page's mobile breakpoint often already handles most of what 1.4.10 Reflow requires, if it exists and actually works.

prompt: A calendar/scheduling grid (days across the top, hours down the side, appointments placed at their intersection) requires horizontal scrolling at 400% zoom. True or false: this is a legitimate reflow exception.

config.statement: A calendar grid with days and hours as its two axes is a legitimate exception to WCAG 1.4.10 Reflow.
config.rubric: Explains that the grid's two axes carry genuine meaning (which day, which hour) that a single column would lose.

hints: Ask the same test as the lesson's schedule-table example: would forcing this into one column destroy the actual relationship between day and time?
This is structurally the same shape as the data-table exception, just rendered as a calendar rather than rows and columns of numbers.
explanation: True — a calendar grid is genuinely two-dimensional in meaning: which day an appointment falls on and what time it starts are both essential, simultaneous facts that a single-column layout would have to either lose or express through much more cumbersome means. This is functionally the same exception as a data table, just visually presented as a grid of days and hours rather than rows and columns of figures.

prompt: Match each WCAG criterion to what it actually tests.

pairs.right: No two-dimensional scrolling for ordinary content at 400% zoom
Content survives increased line-height, letter-spacing and word-spacing without clipping or overlap
Meaning never depends on color as the only distinguisher
Icons, borders and UI components meet a 3:1 contrast ratio

hints: These four are easy to blur together since they're all "low vision" related — the drill is keeping which one tests what straight.
Two of them are about zoom/size, one is about color meaning, one is about non-text contrast specifically.
explanation: Four genuinely separate requirements, each catching a different real failure mode: Reflow is about scroll axes at high zoom, Text Spacing is about surviving increased spacing at the same size, Use of Color is about meaning never depending solely on color, and Non-text Contrast is specifically about icons and UI components (not body text) clearing 3:1. A component can pass three of these and fail the fourth completely, which is exactly why a real audit checks each one independently rather than treating "low vision" as one undifferentiated check.

prompt: Sort each finding into the WCAG criterion it most directly belongs to.

items.text: A fixed-width sidebar forces horizontal scrolling to read the main article text at 400% zoom
A card's badge text overlaps its border the moment letter-spacing is increased via an accessibility extension
A form marks required fields only by making the label text red, with no asterisk or other indicator
A pricing table's plan names get clipped mid-word when line-height increases to 1.5×

hints: Zoom/scroll-axis problems go to Reflow; spacing-override clipping goes to Text Spacing; color-as-the-only-signal goes to Use of Color.
Two of these four are text-spacing failures with the same underlying pattern (fixed-height container, no room to grow) applied to different components.
explanation: The sidebar/scroll-axis issue is a reflow problem; both clipping cases are text-spacing failures sharing the same root cause (a rigid container with no room to grow); the red-only required-field marker is a use-of-color problem, since the meaning depends entirely on perceiving that one color. Recognizing the shared root cause behind superficially different-looking findings — two components, one underlying CSS pattern — is exactly the kind of pattern-matching a real audit rewards.

prompt: Put these steps in order for diagnosing why a magnifier user reports a multi-step form "just stopped working" after step 3.

items: Reproduce the flow yourself with a screen magnifier at 300%, focus-tracking mode on
Complete steps 1 through 3 exactly as the user described
At step 3, check whether anything changed on the page (an error, a confirmation, a new field) outside the current magnified viewport
If something changed off-screen, confirm whether focus was moved to it or whether it just silently appeared elsewhere
State the fix: move focus to the new or changed content programmatically, so a focus-tracking viewport follows it there

hints: This mirrors the worked-example diagnostic order from the lesson — reproduce first, then check location relative to viewport, then check whether focus moved.
The fix is almost always the same one: move focus to wherever the important change happened.
explanation: Reproducing the exact reported flow first rules out an unrelated cause; checking what changed and where relative to the current viewport is the actual diagnostic step; and the fix — moving focus to new or changed content — is the same mechanism that recurs across this whole phase for screen reader, keyboard and magnifier users alike.

prompt: A custom radio-button group shows the selected option purely by changing the option's text color to blue, with the same circle outline for every option. What happens under forced-colours mode?

options.text: All options become visually identical, since the text-color change was the only signal and forced-colours overrides it
Nothing changes — forced colours doesn't affect radio buttons specifically
The selected option becomes bold automatically as a fallback

hints: This is the same pattern as the checkbox example from the lesson, applied to a radio group instead.
There's no automatic fallback styling that forced-colours mode adds on its own — if nothing else distinguishes the states, nothing will.
explanation: All options become indistinguishable — text color is precisely the kind of author-specified color property forced-colours overrides, and with the same circle outline used for every option regardless of selection state, nothing survives to show which one is actually selected. The fix follows the same pattern as the checkbox: a filled/unfilled circle (a shape change, not just a color change) or an explicit forced-colors fallback using a system color keyword.

prompt: A teammate says: "I checked contrast on our whole design system and everything passes." What specific follow-up questions would you ask before trusting that this covers low-vision users adequately?
hints: Contrast ratio is only one of at least four separate things this module covers — what else hasn't been mentioned?
"Everything passes" — passes what threshold, on what size of text, checked against what background?
Ask specifically about reflow, text spacing, and forced colours, none of which "contrast passes" would tell you anything about.
explanation: Strong follow-ups: which threshold was applied to which text (was large text correctly given 3:1, or was everything checked against the stricter 4.5:1, potentially hiding a real failure the other direction), was non-text UI (icons, borders, focus indicators) checked separately under 1.4.11, and was use-of-color checked at all, since that's a completely different criterion contrast ratio says nothing about. Beyond contrast specifically: was reflow at 400% zoom tested, was a text-spacing override tested, was forced-colours mode tested — "contrast passes" answers exactly one of at least five separate questions a real low-vision pass needs answered.

prompt: A component passes both 1.4.10 Reflow and 1.4.3 Contrast. True or false: it's therefore reasonably safe to assume it also handles text-spacing overrides and forced-colours mode correctly.

config.statement: Passing reflow and contrast checks reasonably implies a component also handles text spacing and forced colours correctly.
config.rubric: Explains that these are four independent failure modes with different causes, and passing some says nothing about the others.

hints: Each of the four criteria in this module targets a genuinely different CSS mechanism — a component can be immune to one and completely vulnerable to another.
Think of a specific real example from this module where a component passes zoom cleanly and still shatters under something else.
explanation: False. The card-title example from this module passed perfectly well at default spacing and under normal zoom, and still clipped text the instant a 1.4.12 text-spacing override was applied — a completely independent failure mode from reflow or contrast. Forced-colours failures are independent again, tied to color-only state indicators rather than font size or spacing at all. Each of these four checks targets a different mechanism, and a real low-vision pass has to run all of them separately, not infer three from one.

prompt: A page has a well-labeled main navigation region and a well-labeled main content region, each containing several controls. Under row-column switch scanning, what does this grouping actually buy a user?

options.text: A first-level choice between the two regions, so a control in "main content" doesn't require scanning through every control in the navigation first
Nothing — row-column scanning ignores landmarks entirely and always scans every control in strict document order
It only changes the visual highlight color, not the actual scan order

hints: Row-column scanning needs real groups to organize by — this is exactly the mechanism landmarks provide.
Think about the difference between scanning through everything in order versus picking a region first, then scanning only within it.
explanation: Landmark regions (or headings, or fieldsets) give row-column scanning real groups to present as a first choice — pick the region, then scan only within it, instead of stepping through every control in the whole page's document order. This is the same structural markup from the keyboard and screen reader modules doing a third, mechanically distinct job here: cutting real wait time for a switch user, on top of skip-navigation and landmark-jump benefits for keyboard and screen reader users.

prompt: A settings page has forty toggles, ungrouped, in a flat list. A developer argues this is fine because "switch users can just set a faster scan speed." True or false: a faster scan speed solves this problem.

config.statement: Increasing switch scan speed resolves the cost of a large, ungrouped control list.
config.rubric: Explains that scan speed changes the per-step cost, not the number of steps — grouping is what reduces step count.

hints: Scan speed controls how long each highlight-step takes, not how many steps exist between the start and the target.
A faster scan also raises the precision required to hit the switch at the right moment — it's not a free improvement.
explanation: False. Scan speed changes how long each individual step takes, not how many steps exist — a forty-item flat list still requires up to forty steps to reach the last item, just faster ones. Faster scanning also demands more precise timing from the user, which isn't free for someone whose motor control is already limited; it can trade one difficulty for another rather than removing it. Real grouping (fieldsets, headings, landmarks) is what actually reduces the number of steps, which is the only fix that addresses the root cause rather than compensating for it.

prompt: A close ("X") button is 18×18 CSS pixels, but sits with generous empty space around it — large enough that a 24px circle centered on it wouldn't overlap any neighboring target's equivalent circle. Does this meet WCAG 2.5.8?

options.text: Yes — this is exactly the spacing exception: a smaller target can still pass if enough surrounding space compensates for the reduced size
No — 18px always fails regardless of spacing
Yes, but only because it's a close/dismiss button specifically, which is always exempt

hints: This is the exact spacing-exception scenario from the lesson — size and spacing trade off against each other.
There's no button-type-based exemption in the criterion — the exemptions are about spacing, inline text links, and equivalent-alternative availability, not what the button does.
explanation: Yes, this qualifies for the spacing exception described in the lesson — a target under 24px can still pass 2.5.8 if the space around it is generous enough that equivalent circles wouldn't overlap. There's no separate "close buttons are exempt" rule; this passes specifically because of the measured spacing, not because of what kind of control it is.

prompt: A row of five social-share icon buttons are each 16×16px with 2px gaps between them. Write this up as a finding: what fails, why it matters beyond "the number is too small," and a concrete fix.
hints: State the measured size and gap against the actual 24px threshold and the spacing-exception math, not just "looks small."
Think about who specifically is affected and what the real-world cost of a mis-tap is here (probably low-stakes for social share, compared to the earlier delete-button example — say so honestly).
The fix should be concrete: a specific new size and/or gap, not "make it bigger."
explanation: A strong finding measures precisely: 16×16px is under the 24px minimum, and 2px gaps are nowhere near enough to qualify for the spacing exception (which needs roughly the equivalent of a 24px-diameter buffer). It names who's affected — anyone with a tremor, limited fine motor control, or simply using a touchscreen with an imprecise fingertip — and is honest that the real-world cost here (accidentally sharing to the wrong platform) is lower-stakes than, say, the earlier delete-button example, without treating that as a reason to skip the finding. The fix is concrete: increase each target to at least 24×24px, or keep the visual icon smaller while padding the actual clickable/tappable area out to 24px and adding real spacing between them.

prompt: A custom icon-only "share" button has no aria-label, no title, and no text content — only an SVG icon. What happens when a voice control user says "click share"?

options.text: Nothing matches — the command fails, since the button has no accessible name for "share" (or anything else) to match against
Voice control recognizes the icon's visual meaning and clicks it correctly
It works, but only if the user says the exact SVG filename instead

hints: This is the exact same accessible-name gap from the semantics module, now costing a second assistive technology.
Voice control has no way to interpret an icon's visual meaning — it needs actual computed text to match against.
explanation: The command fails — with no accessible name computed for this button, there's nothing for "click share" to match against, regardless of how visually obvious the share icon is to a sighted user. This is precisely the same accessible-name gap the semantics module covered, now shown to break a second, completely independent assistive technology for the identical underlying reason.

prompt: A page has three "Edit" buttons, one per row in a table, each with an accessible name of just "Edit." True or false: a screen reader finding about this would automatically also cover the voice control impact.

config.statement: A finding written for screen reader disorientation caused by duplicate names automatically covers the voice control impact of the same duplicate names.
config.rubric: Explains that the two mechanisms of harm are different (disorientation vs. broken command) and a complete finding should name both explicitly, even though the fix is shared.

hints: Disorientation (screen reader) and a broken/ambiguous command (voice control) are two different kinds of harm, even from the identical root cause.
A report that only mentions one assistive technology risks under-selling the severity, since the voice control impact is arguably worse here.
explanation: False, in the sense that matters for a complete report — the fix is identical (unique, distinguishing names), but the two mechanisms of harm are genuinely different: a screen reader user hears "Edit" three times and can work out which one they're on through other context; a voice control user saying "click Edit" gets a straightforwardly broken or ambiguous command. Naming both impacts explicitly, rather than assuming a screen-reader-framed finding implicitly covers voice control too, gives a developer the full picture of why the fix matters and how many different real users it actually protects.

prompt: A support team insists their 60-second inactivity logout can't be changed because it's "required for security." What's the strongest, most specific pushback per WCAG 2.2.1's essential exception?

options.text: Ask what specific security property breaks if the timeout instead warns the user twenty seconds before expiry and lets them extend it — warn-and-extend serves most real security goals without excluding slower input methods
Accept it as-is; "security" is always a valid essential exception under 2.2.1
Insist the timeout be removed completely, since any time limit is inherently inaccessible

hints: The essential exception is narrow and has to be argued for specifically, not invoked as a blanket justification.
The fix this module recommends isn't "no timeout at all" — it's warn-and-extend, which usually satisfies both the security goal and the accessibility requirement.
explanation: Pushing back with a specific question — what security property actually breaks under warn-and-extend — is the productive move, because "security" is claimed as an essential exception far more often than it genuinely qualifies, and warn-and-extend (rather than removing timeouts entirely) usually preserves whatever real security goal existed while meeting 2.2.1. Accepting the claim uncritically or demanding the timeout be eliminated outright are both weaker positions than asking the specific question that tests whether the exception genuinely applies.

prompt: Sort each time limit into whether it likely qualifies for a WCAG 2.2.1 exception, or needs an adjust/extend/warn mechanism.

items.text: A live auction's bidding window, closing at a fixed real-world time shared by all bidders
A 90-second inactivity logout on a multi-step account settings form
A timed typing-speed test, where completing it quickly is literally the skill being measured
A checkout page's "complete your order within 5:00" countdown with no extend option

hints: The two genuine exceptions from the lesson are real-time events and limits essential to what's being measured — everything else needs the adjust/extend/warn mechanism.
A checkout countdown isn't measuring anything about the user's speed — it's a business decision that happens to impose a time limit.
explanation: The auction and the typing-speed test both fit the narrow, genuine exceptions: one is a real-time event shared across users, the other's entire point is measuring completion speed. The account settings timeout and the checkout countdown are both ordinary content-imposed limits with no such justification — exactly the kind of "security" or "business need" framing this lesson names as rarely holding up to the actual essential-exception test.

prompt: Put these steps in order for testing a drag-to-reorder list for WCAG 2.5.7 compliance.

items: Attempt to reorder an item using only a mouse drag, confirming the drag itself works
Look for any non-drag alternative — buttons, a menu option, arrow-key reordering — anywhere in the interface
If no alternative exists, confirm this by trying to reorder with keyboard-only and switch/voice-simulated input
Determine whether dragging is essential to the function (a freehand drawing tool) or just the only method offered for an otherwise ordinary action (reordering a list)
Log the finding: no single-pointer alternative exists for a non-essential drag interaction, citing 2.5.7

hints: Confirm the drag itself works first — this rules out a completely broken feature versus a missing-alternative one.
The essential/non-essential judgment call comes after confirming no alternative exists, since it's what determines whether this is actually a defect.
explanation: Confirming the drag itself works establishes a baseline; searching for an alternative and then testing without a mouse confirms whether one genuinely doesn't exist; and the essential-function judgment is what separates a real 2.5.7 finding (ordinary reordering, drag-only) from a legitimate exception (a drawing tool, where dragging is the entire point).

prompt: A tooltip appears both on :hover and on :focus (keyboard Tab), fixing the original hover-only defect. True or false: this alone fully satisfies WCAG 1.4.13 Content on Hover or Focus.

config.statement: Triggering hover-revealed content on both :hover and :focus is, by itself, sufficient to fully meet WCAG 1.4.13.
config.rubric: Names at least one of the other sub-requirements from the lesson — dismissible, hoverable (stays visible when the pointer moves onto it), or persistent — that also has to be met.

hints: The lesson named three separate sub-requirements once hover-revealed content exists at all — triggering it correctly is only the starting point.
Think about what happens if the tooltip vanishes the instant the mouse moves toward it, or can't be dismissed without moving focus away entirely.
explanation: False. Triggering the content on both hover and focus fixes the operability gap (can it be opened at all without a mouse), but 1.4.13 also requires the revealed content to be dismissible (typically via Escape), to remain visible while the user's pointer moves onto the revealed content itself, and to persist rather than disappearing the instant it appears. A tooltip that now opens on Tab but vanishes if the mouse so much as approaches it, or that can't be closed without tabbing away entirely, still fails 1.4.13 even after the hover/focus fix — three genuinely separate sub-requirements, not one.

prompt: Two pages have the same 50 interactive elements. Page A groups them under five labeled fieldsets; Page B has them in one flat, ungrouped sequence. Under row-column switch scanning, which is faster to operate?

options.text: Page A — grouping lets the scan pick a fieldset first, then scan only its handful of controls, instead of stepping through all 50 in sequence
They're equally fast — total control count is all that matters, not grouping
Page B — flat sequences are always faster because there's only one level to navigate

hints: This is the exact mechanism from the module's first lesson — real grouping gives row-column scanning something to organize by.
"One level to navigate" sounds simpler but actually means every single control costs a full step, with no shortcut.
explanation: Page A — real grouping is precisely what turns a worst case of fifty sequential steps into roughly (number of groups) plus (controls within the one selected group), a dramatic reduction for anyone using row-column scanning specifically.

prompt: An inline text link inside a paragraph, styled at the surrounding text's normal size (well under 24px tall), is flagged as a 2.5.8 Target Size violation. True or false: this is a correct finding.

config.statement: An inline text link within a paragraph, smaller than 24px, is correctly flagged as a 2.5.8 Target Size violation.
config.rubric: Names the inline-text-link exception specifically, distinguishing it from a standalone button or icon target.

hints: This is one of the specific, named exceptions from the lesson — not a general size loophole.
Think about what a 24px minimum would do to ordinary paragraph text if it applied to every inline link.
explanation: False — inline text links within a block of text are one of 2.5.8's explicit exceptions, precisely because applying a 24px minimum to every link inside ordinary paragraph text would be impractical and would fight against normal typography rather than serving a real accessibility purpose. The 24px requirement is squarely aimed at standalone targets — buttons, icons, form controls — not links embedded in running text.

prompt: Match each WCAG criterion from this module to what it actually tests.

pairs.right: Pointer targets are at least 24×24px, or compensated for with spacing
A drag-based interaction has a single-pointer, non-drag alternative
A content-imposed time limit can be turned off, extended, or warns before expiry
Hover/focus-revealed content is dismissible, stays visible when the pointer reaches it, and persists

hints: These four are easy to blur together since they're all motor/timing-adjacent — the drill is keeping which one governs what specifically.
Two are about pointer precision and gesture, two are about time and revealed content.
explanation: Four genuinely separate, specific requirements: target size is about a control's physical dimensions, dragging movements is about needing a non-drag path to the same result, timing adjustable is about user control over content-imposed clocks, and content on hover/focus is about what has to be true of anything a hover or focus event reveals. A component can satisfy three of these and fail the fourth completely, which is why a real review checks each independently.

prompt: Sort each finding into which input method(s) it primarily excludes.

items.text: A settings page with 80 ungrouped toggles in one flat scan sequence
Six identically-named "Add to cart" buttons on a product listing page
A drag-only file reorder with no button-based alternative and no accessible name issues
A hover-only submenu with no click, focus or keyboard alternative at all

hints: A pure scan-order/count problem (nothing wrong with any individual control's name) is specifically a switch-access cost.
A pure naming-ambiguity problem (control count and grouping are both fine) is specifically a voice-control problem.
Drag-only and hover-only interactions block the underlying gesture itself, which neither switch access nor voice control can perform regardless of how well-named or well-grouped anything is.
explanation: The ungrouped toggle page is a pure scan-cost problem — nothing about naming is broken, so voice control users aren't specifically affected the same way. The duplicate "Add to cart" buttons are a pure naming-ambiguity problem — control count and grouping aren't the issue, so switch scanning itself isn't specifically slower. Drag-only and hover-only interactions block the underlying gesture itself, which neither switch access (no continuous-drag or hover concept) nor voice control (unreliable drag emulation, no reliable hover trigger) can perform, regardless of how well everything else is built.

prompt: Put these steps in order for diagnosing a checkout countdown timer's WCAG 2.2.1 compliance.

items: Confirm a content-imposed time limit exists and note its duration
Check whether the interface offers any way to turn it off, extend it, or receive a warning before expiry
If none exists, check whether the limit is a genuine real-time event or essential to what's being measured
If it's neither of those, log it as a 2.2.1 finding citing the missing adjust/extend/warn mechanism
Recommend a specific fix: a visible warning at least 20 seconds before expiry with a keyboard/switch/voice-operable extend control

hints: This mirrors the categorization drill's logic — confirm the limit, check for a mechanism, then check for a genuine exception before concluding it's a defect.
The fix should be specific enough that a developer doesn't have to guess at what "adjustable" means in practice.
explanation: This is the same diagnostic order the lesson used: confirm the limit exists, check for any adjust/extend/warn mechanism, and only then evaluate whether a genuine exception applies — skipping straight to "log a finding" without checking for the essential exception first risks a false alarm on a legitimately exempt real-time event or skills test.

prompt: A voice control user says "click menu" on a page with a single, correctly-named hamburger menu button. It opens correctly. What does this confirm, and what does it NOT confirm?

options.text: It confirms the button's accessible name works for voice matching — it does NOT confirm anything about the items inside the menu once opened, which need their own names checked separately
It confirms the entire page is voice-control accessible
It confirms the menu is also accessible to switch and screen reader users

hints: One successful voice command tells you about exactly one control — not the rest of the page, and not the menu's own contents once it opens.
Each assistive technology (switch, voice, screen reader) has to be checked independently — success with one doesn't imply success with the others.
explanation: One working command confirms exactly one thing: this specific button has a usable accessible name for voice matching. It says nothing about the menu items that appear once it opens (each needs its own checkable name), nothing about the rest of the page's controls, and nothing about switch or screen reader compatibility, which depend on different mechanisms entirely (scan grouping, focus/announcement behavior) that a single successful voice command doesn't test at all.

prompt: A teammate says: "Our app doesn't need switch or voice control testing — we don't have any users who use those." How would you respond, using what this whole phase has established?
hints: Think about how many of this module's findings are also keyboard or screen reader findings in disguise (unnamed controls, hover-only content, missing focus management).
Consider the foundations phase's point about situational and temporary access needs — who acquires a motor impairment temporarily, not permanently.
"We don't have users who need X" is a claim that's very hard to actually verify, and usually isn't the point anyway.
explanation: A strong response draws on several threads from across this whole phase: many switch/voice findings are the same underlying defect (missing accessible names, hover-only triggers, no focus management) that also break keyboard and screen reader access — fixing them once serves multiple audiences simultaneously, so the marginal cost of testing for switch/voice specifically is often lower than it sounds. It's also nearly impossible to actually know "we have zero users who need this" — temporary injuries, situational limitations (holding a baby, driving), and undisclosed conditions mean the claim is unverifiable in practice, exactly the situational-and-temporary-access-needs point from the foundations phase. The stronger framing isn't "you're wrong, you do have these users" — it's "the fixes for this are largely shared with keyboard and screen reader access you're already committed to, so the actual incremental cost of doing this properly is smaller than the framing suggests."

prompt: A product passes every keyboard-only test from the keyboard module and every screen reader test from the screen reader module. True or false: it's therefore reasonably safe to assume it also works well for switch and voice control users.

config.statement: Passing keyboard-only and screen reader testing reasonably implies a product also works well for switch and voice control users.
config.rubric: Names at least one mechanism specific to switch or voice (scan-order cost, target size, voice-name ambiguity) that neither keyboard nor screen reader testing would surface.

hints: Keyboard testing doesn't measure how many Tab-stops something takes, only whether Tab eventually reaches it — switch scanning cares specifically about the count.
Screen reader testing checks whether a name is announced correctly, not whether it's ambiguous against five other identical names in a way that breaks voice matching specifically.
Target size and timing barriers aren't covered by either keyboard or screen reader testing at all.
explanation: False. Keyboard testing confirms Tab eventually reaches every control, but says nothing about how many steps that took — which is exactly what determines switch-scanning cost. Screen reader testing confirms a name is announced correctly, but doesn't test whether that name is ambiguous against five identical siblings in a way that specifically breaks voice-command matching. And neither keyboard nor screen reader testing touches target size, spacing, or drag-only interactions at all — this module's mechanisms are genuinely additional, not a subset of what the earlier two already covered, which is exactly why the phase dedicates a full separate module to them.
